summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: almost every video gets 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 60 views. The best performers are short 'X doesn't do what you think, it only does Y' videos about a single sensor or robot (clap switch, gyro robot, line follower), and the clap switch ones also did well on YouTube. Generic 'How does X work?' questions (lifts, taps, smoke alarms, street lights) get few views and almost no likes, shares or saves, and the one English video and videos with no Instagram numbers did poorly.
winningPattern: A single-sensor or robot subject with a surprising 'it doesn't do X, it only does Y' or 'without it, this robot fails' hook, written in Hinglish with one emoji and #shorts. Titles are short, a bold claim rather than a question. They are posted on Instagram Reels first, and the clap-switch and gyro-robot topics also work on YouTube. Maker-style hands-on demos (robot, clap switch, DHT11, mic) get the most likes, saves and shares.
doMore: Lead with a counterintuitive claim: 'X doesn't do A, it only does B'
Pick one hands-on maker demo per video (robot, clap switch, DHT11, mic) rather than everyday gadgets
Post to Instagram first, since it reliably gets 1,000+ views, then cross-post to YouTube
Make follow-ups to the winners: a gyro/balancing robot series and clap-switch variations
Add a save-worthy ending, like a wiring tip or pin-out, to boost saves and shares
stopDoing: Generic 'How does X work?' questions about public gadgets (lift, tap, smoke alarm, street light)
Posting several near-duplicate videos on the same sensor within days (IR, PIR, smoke, tap)
Publishing to YouTube only or in English, since those got almost no reach
